rituals.name: DISASTER TRAILER CUT

rituals.mission: Give the worry the movie trailer it has clearly been auditioning for.
rituals.rule: Guess which version will feel more dangerous: the dramatic trailer or the boring CCTV cut.

rituals.mind_bend: The problem may be real. The director’s cut in your head is optional.

rituals.name: CAPTION WITHOUT ADJECTIVES
rituals.goal: Let’s see how much emotional weight is hiding inside descriptive words.
rituals.mission: Let’s see how much emotional weight is hiding inside descriptive words.
rituals.rule: Guess whether the story will feel weaker, stronger, or identical after the adjectives disappear.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether the story will feel weaker, stronger, or identical after the adjectives disappear.
rituals.play: Say the thought once. Now remove words like awful, humiliating, impossible, terrible, rude, disastrous, pathetic. Keep only nouns, verbs, times and places.
rituals.twist: Listen to what survives when the emotional colouring is stripped out.
rituals.mindBend: A feeling can be real without its explanation being right.
rituals.mind_bend: A feeling can be real without its explanation being right.
rituals.why: Adjectives often smuggle a verdict into a description.
rituals.reveal: Adjectives often smuggle a verdict into a description.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use the sentence to test meaning, not to suppress emotion. A feeling can remain present while you leave its explanation open. Stop at the planned endpoint rather than repeating the ritual until it feels completely convincing.

rituals.name: MISSING CAMERA ANGLE
rituals.goal: You have one camera angle and your brain has already written everyone else’s dialogue.
rituals.mission: You have one camera angle and your brain has already written everyone else’s dialogue.
rituals.rule: Guess how many plausible explanations you can create without changing the visible facts.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how many plausible explanations you can create without changing the visible facts.
rituals.play: Picture three unseen angles: behind them, five minutes before, five minutes after. Give each one plausible detail.
rituals.twist: Notice how easily the meaning changes when hidden context changes.
rituals.mindBend: What you cannot see is exactly where certainty likes to invent furniture.
rituals.mind_bend: What you cannot see is exactly where certainty likes to invent furniture.
rituals.why: The original interpretation was one camera angle, not the whole set.
rituals.reveal: The original interpretation was one camera angle, not the whole set.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use the mental image to reduce mind-reading, not to manufacture reassurance. Direct communication and boundaries carry more weight than guessed motives. Leave room for new evidence after the exercise instead of treating the result as final.

rituals.name: PREDICTION TIMESTAMP
rituals.goal: Your future thought arrived without a date stamp.
rituals.mission: Your future thought arrived without a date stamp.
rituals.rule: Guess whether the sentence feels different after you attach the exact future time it claims to know.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether the sentence feels different after you attach the exact future time it claims to know.
rituals.play: Add a timestamp to the prediction: “At 3:20 pm tomorrow, I predict…” Say the whole sentence again with the timestamp.
rituals.twist: Check if it sounds more like a forecast and less like a fact happening now.
rituals.mindBend: A forecast is not evidence from the future. It is a guess made in the present.
rituals.mind_bend: A forecast is not evidence from the future. It is a guess made in the present.
rituals.why: Time-stamping forces a prediction back into the future where it belongs.
rituals.reveal: Time-stamping forces a prediction back into the future where it belongs.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE

rituals.name: REVERSE PROSECUTOR
rituals.goal: For twenty seconds, your current theory loses its lawyer.
rituals.mission: For twenty seconds, your current theory loses its lawyer.
rituals.rule: Guess how hard it will be to argue the opposite explanation using the same facts.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how hard it will be to argue the opposite explanation using the same facts.

rituals.twist: Check if the “impossible” opposite becomes surprisingly easy to defend.
rituals.mindBend: Your first explanation may be convincing without being exclusive.
rituals.mind_bend: Your first explanation may be convincing without being exclusive.
rituals.why: If the same evidence can support two stories, the evidence did not uniquely prove the first one.
rituals.reveal: If the same evidence can support two stories, the evidence did not uniquely prove the first one.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE

rituals.name: THREE MEANINGS, SAME EVENT
rituals.goal: Same event. Three meanings. Let’s see which part is actually glued to reality.
rituals.mission: Same event. Three meanings. Let’s see which part is actually glued to reality.
rituals.rule: Guess whether you can make the event mean three different things without changing what happened.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether you can make the event mean three different things without changing what happened.

rituals.twist: Notice that the facts stayed still while the emotional meaning moved.
rituals.mindBend: Events happen once. Meaning can be edited more than once.
rituals.mind_bend: Events happen once. Meaning can be edited more than once.

rituals.name: IDENTITY JACKET
rituals.goal: Take “I am” off for a second.
rituals.mission: Take “I am” off for a second.
rituals.rule: Guess which sentence feels heavier: “I am a failure” or “I’m noticing failure thoughts today.”
rituals.one_rule: Guess which sentence feels heavier: “I am a failure” or “I’m noticing failure thoughts today.”

rituals.mind_bend: A state can visit you without becoming your surname.
rituals.why: Grammar can quietly turn a passing state into a definition of the whole person.

rituals.name: FIVE-YEAR MUSEUM LABEL
rituals.goal: Imagine this problem behind glass five years from now.
rituals.mission: Imagine this problem behind glass five years from now.
rituals.rule: Guess what the museum label will mention—and what it will leave out.
rituals.one_rule: Guess what the museum label will mention—and what it will leave out.
rituals.play: Write a two-line label from five years ahead: “Object: the thing I was stressed about in 2026. What mattered later: ____.” Keep it factual, not inspirational.
rituals.twist: Notice what shrinks when the time horizon expands.
rituals.mindBend: Important now does not automatically mean important forever.
rituals.mind_bend: Important now does not automatically mean important forever.
rituals.why: Distance changes the size of details without claiming they are meaningless now.
rituals.reveal: Distance changes the size of details without claiming they are meaningless now.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use the written version as a test, not a verdict. Stop if you begin forcing the result or using it to ignore information that clearly needs action. Keep the result tied to this one example rather than generalising it to every situation.

rituals.name: TINY ENOUGH TO MATTER
rituals.goal: Pick something so small your ambition feels mildly insulted.
rituals.mission: Pick something so small your ambition feels mildly insulted.
rituals.rule: Guess whether a thirty-second action can still count as living a value.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether a thirty-second action can still count as living a value.
rituals.play: Choose one value—care, courage, learning, honesty, health, creativity. Do the smallest visible action that matches it in under 30 sec.
rituals.twist: Check whether the action becomes meaningless merely because it was tiny.
rituals.mindBend: A compass still works when you only take one step.
rituals.mind_bend: A compass still works when you only take one step.
rituals.why: Values describe direction, not minimum order size.
rituals.reveal: Values describe direction, not minimum order size.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the chosen example small, reversible and safe. Do not use momentum as a reason to ignore pain, exhaustion, major consequences or information that needs more thought. Stop at the planned endpoint rather than repeating the ritual until it feels completely convincing.

rituals.goal: Some rules are alive only because nobody held the funeral.
rituals.mission: Some rules are alive only because nobody held the funeral.
rituals.rule: Guess where this rule came from before you decide whether it still belongs to you.
rituals.one_rule: Guess where this rule came from before you decide whether it still belongs to you.

rituals.twist: Check if the rule still has a current job or only an old origin story.
rituals.mindBend: Old instructions can expire even when they were once useful.
rituals.mind_bend: Old instructions can expire even when they were once useful.
rituals.why: A rule can be inherited without being chosen.
rituals.reveal: A rule can be inherited without being chosen.

rituals.name: BORROWED GOAL DETECTOR
rituals.goal: Let’s check whether this goal is yours or merely renting space in your calendar.
rituals.mission: Let’s check whether this goal is yours or merely renting space in your calendar.
rituals.rule: Guess whose reaction matters most if you imagine quitting the goal tomorrow.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whose reaction matters most if you imagine quitting the goal tomorrow.
rituals.play: Imagine quietly stopping. Who appears first in your mind looking disappointed, impressed, confused or relieved? Name them. Ask what you would still want if nobody ever found out.
rituals.twist: Notice the gap between the audience goal and the private goal.
rituals.mindBend: If nobody could clap, what would still be worth doing?
rituals.mind_bend: If nobody could clap, what would still be worth doing?
rituals.why: Approval can power a goal without making the goal personally meaningful.
rituals.reveal: Approval can power a goal without making the goal personally meaningful.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE

rituals.goal: Do one decent thing nobody can reward you for.

rituals.rule: Guess whether it will feel pointless if nobody sees it.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether it will feel pointless if nobody sees it.

rituals.twist: Check if the action still feels aligned even without social proof.
rituals.mindBend: Some of the most honest choices are the ones that cannot earn applause.
rituals.mind_bend: Some of the most honest choices are the ones that cannot earn applause.
rituals.why: Visibility and value are different currencies.

rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the chosen example on the interpretation, not the other person's rights or limits. A kinder explanation does not cancel a clear no, repeated harm or needed distance. Keep the result tied to this one example rather than generalising it to every situation.

rituals.challenge: Thought monopolising attention
rituals.recognition_cue: Thought monopolising attention
rituals.theory_backbone: Attentional control; orienting response; working memory interference
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Track three dynamic external-state changes, then test verbatim recall of the pre-task thought.
rituals.ritualText:
PLAY TIME
55 sec

GAME
THREE CHANGES

GOAL
Find one thing already moving.

ONE RULE
Guess whether you can follow it through three changes without losing the thought completely.

PLAY
Pick a cursor, fan, shadow, leaf, person, reflection—anything moving. Track three changes: direction, speed, shape, position, brightness.

TWIST
Now try to recall the exact wording of the thought from before the third change.

MIND BEND
Your thought didn’t disappear. It just lost exclusive access to you.

SAFETY
PAUSE
Treat the chosen example as a memory exercise, not a reconstruction of objective proof. Do not fill missing detail just to make the story coherent. Keep the result tied to this one example rather than generalising it to every situation.

rituals.name: PERIPHERAL DOOR
rituals.goal: Stress loves a tunnel.
rituals.mission: Stress loves a tunnel.
rituals.rule: Guess how many objects you can notice at the edges without moving your head.

rituals.mind_bend: A narrowed mind often arrives with a narrowed field of view.

rituals.name: SOUND UNTIL IT CHANGES
rituals.goal: Choose one sound and wait for it to betray its own sameness.
rituals.mission: Choose one sound and wait for it to betray its own sameness.
rituals.rule: Guess how long it will stay exactly the same.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how long it will stay exactly the same.
rituals.play: Pick a continuous sound: aircon, traffic, hum, rain, fridge. Listen only for the first change in pitch, volume, rhythm or distance.
rituals.twist: Catch the moment “constant” becomes obviously variable.
rituals.mindBend: What feels continuous is often changing underneath your label for it.
rituals.mind_bend: What feels continuous is often changing underneath your label for it.
rituals.why: Attention reveals micro-changes that a stressed brain compresses into “this is just how it is.”
rituals.reveal: Attention reveals micro-changes that a stressed brain compresses into “this is just how it is.”
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the chosen example to one brief experiment. If it starts making you less steady, more confused or more stuck, stop and return to the concrete facts in front of you. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.

rituals.name: TEMPERATURE COIN
rituals.goal: Touch something cool or warm and make a prediction before your skin votes.
rituals.mission: Touch something cool or warm and make a prediction before your skin votes.
rituals.rule: Guess how many seconds the strongest sensation will last.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how many seconds the strongest sensation will last.
rituals.play: Touch a safe cool or warm object for one second. Remove it. Count slowly until the sensation changes category—strong to mild, sharp to vague, local to spread.
rituals.twist: Compare the predicted duration with the actual change point.
rituals.mindBend: A sensation can be intense without being stable.
rituals.mind_bend: A sensation can be intense without being stable.
rituals.why: Body sensations are dynamic, and prediction often overestimates how fixed they will feel.
rituals.reveal: Body sensations are dynamic, and prediction often overestimates how fixed they will feel.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use only comfortably mild temperatures and brief skin contact—no ice, very hot objects or prolonged exposure. Stop with pain, numbness, burning, or a lasting change in skin colour.

rituals.name: JAW CONTRAST
rituals.goal: Make tension obvious on purpose so release has something to compare with.
rituals.mission: Make tension obvious on purpose so release has something to compare with.
rituals.rule: Guess whether your jaw is already closer to “soft” or “clenched.”
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether your jaw is already closer to “soft” or “clenched.”
rituals.play: Gently clench your jaw for three seconds—no pain—then let it hang loose. Do nothing else.
rituals.twist: Notice which state suddenly becomes easier to identify because you created contrast.
rituals.mindBend: Sometimes calm is easier to find after you show the body what “not calm” feels like.
rituals.mind_bend: Sometimes calm is easier to find after you show the body what “not calm” feels like.
rituals.why: The nervous system notices differences better than vague instructions to “relax.”
rituals.reveal: The nervous system notices differences better than vague instructions to “relax.”
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use only a gentle, short jaw contraction—no hard clenching. Stop for tooth pain, jaw pain, locking, painful clicking or facial discomfort.

rituals.name: THREE SLOW BLINK CUTS
rituals.goal: Your eyes have a built-in edit button.
rituals.mission: Your eyes have a built-in edit button.
rituals.rule: Guess whether three slow blinks will make the scene feel continuous or slightly reset.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether three slow blinks will make the scene feel continuous or slightly reset.
rituals.play: Blink slowly three times. Each time, notice the instant the visual world disappears and returns.
rituals.twist: Catch the tiny “new frame” feeling after each reopening.
rituals.mindBend: The scene feels continuous because your brain edits the cuts out.
rituals.mind_bend: The scene feels continuous because your brain edits the cuts out.
rituals.why: Perception is stitched from interruptions, even when experience feels continuous.
rituals.reveal: Perception is stitched from interruptions, even when experience feels continuous.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Blink gently at your natural pace. Do not squeeze the eyes shut, prolong the blinks or repeat them to chase the visual cut; stop for eye pain, marked dryness, dizziness or unusual visual symptoms.

rituals.name: FOUR CORNERS
rituals.goal: Keep the thought.
rituals.mission: Keep the thought.
rituals.rule: Guess whether the thought can stay present while your eyes visit four corners of the room.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether the thought can stay present while your eyes visit four corners of the room.
rituals.play: Without moving your head much, look to four corners in a slow square. At each corner, name one shape or line.
rituals.twist: Notice the thought and visual task can coexist without either taking over.
rituals.mindBend: A thought can be in the room without becoming the room.
rituals.mind_bend: A thought can be in the room without becoming the room.
rituals.why: Attention can contain a thought without being identical to the thought.

rituals.safety:

rituals.goal: Pick a colour.
rituals.mission: Pick a colour.
rituals.rule: Guess how many objects of that colour you will notice in ten seconds.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how many objects of that colour you will notice in ten seconds.

rituals.mind_bend: What you notice more is not always what exists more.

rituals.name: PULSE WITHOUT A STORY
rituals.goal: Find a body signal and ban the biography for ten seconds.
rituals.mission: Find a body signal and ban the biography for ten seconds.
rituals.rule: Guess whether you can describe the sensation without using an emotion word.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether you can describe the sensation without using an emotion word.
rituals.play: Notice your pulse, chest, throat or stomach. Describe only physical properties: fast, slow, tight, warm, fluttery, heavy, moving. No “anxious,” “bad,” “dangerous,” or “because.”
rituals.twist: Catch how quickly the mind tries to add an explanation.
rituals.mindBend: Your body can send a signal before your story decides what it means.
rituals.mind_bend: Your body can send a signal before your story decides what it means.
rituals.why: Sensation and interpretation arrive close together, but they are not the same event.
rituals.reveal: Sensation and interpretation arrive close together, but they are not the same event.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Do one short observation only; repeated symptom checking can feed the loop. Concerning or persistent physical symptoms are for medical assessment, not self-reassurance.

rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Deliberately suppress target thought briefly to expose monitoring-driven rebound mechanism.
rituals.ritualText:
PLAY TIME
55 sec

GAME
WHITE BEAR’S COUSIN

GOAL
For five seconds, absolutely do not think the thought.

ONE RULE
Guess whether forcefully banning it will make it appear less or more.

PLAY
Set five seconds. Try hard not to think the target thought. The instant it appears, just notice that the ban itself kept checking for it.

TWIST
Catch the monitoring process asking, “Am I thinking it yet?”

MIND BEND
To check that a thought is gone, the brain has to keep looking for it.

SAFETY
PAUSE
Use the timed pass as an interruption, not a new way to rehearse the loop. One deliberate pass is enough. If the same pattern returns later, re-check the new context rather than copying today's answer.

rituals.name: NEW INFORMATION RECEIPT
rituals.goal: If this is problem solving, it should be producing something new.
rituals.mission: If this is problem solving, it should be producing something new.
rituals.rule: Guess how many genuinely new facts appeared in the last three loops.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how many genuinely new facts appeared in the last three loops.
rituals.play: Replay the last three rounds mentally. For each, name one new fact, decision or action that did not exist before. If there is none, mark it “replay.”
rituals.twist: Notice the difference between thinking longer and learning more.
rituals.mindBend: Mental effort is not the same thing as mental progress.
rituals.mind_bend: Mental effort is not the same thing as mental progress.
rituals.why: Repetition can feel effortful without generating information.
rituals.reveal: Repetition can feel effortful without generating information.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE

rituals.name: PUT IT ON THE WALL
rituals.goal: Your thought feels inside your head.
rituals.mission: Your thought feels inside your head.
rituals.rule: Guess where in the room the thought would “sit” if it had to occupy a physical spot.
rituals.one_rule: Guess where in the room the thought would “sit” if it had to occupy a physical spot.
rituals.play: Point to a wall, chair or object and imagine the sentence printed there. Move your eyes to it, then away from it, then back.
rituals.twist: Check if the thought feels like something you can look at instead of live inside.
rituals.mindBend: A thought can be something you notice, not a room you are trapped inside.
rituals.mind_bend: A thought can be something you notice, not a room you are trapped inside.
rituals.why: Spatialising mental content can create a simple sense of distance without denying the content.

rituals.safety:

rituals.name: STOP BEFORE THE LAST WORD
rituals.goal: Your brain hates an unfinished sentence.
rituals.mission: Your brain hates an unfinished sentence.
rituals.rule: Guess how strong the urge will be to complete a familiar loop if you stop one word early.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how strong the urge will be to complete a familiar loop if you stop one word early.
rituals.play: Begin the repeating sentence and deliberately stop before the final word. Hold the blank for five seconds. Don’t fill it.
rituals.twist: Feel the pull to complete the phrase.
rituals.mindBend: Sometimes the loop wants completion, not truth.
rituals.mind_bend: Sometimes the loop wants completion, not truth.

rituals.name: SEARCH BAR TEST
rituals.goal: Would you type this question into a search bar expecting one factual answer?
rituals.mission: Would you type this question into a search bar expecting one factual answer?
rituals.rule: Guess whether the loop is actually asking for information or demanding impossible certainty.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether the loop is actually asking for information or demanding impossible certainty.
rituals.play: Phrase the loop as a search query. Ask: “What observable answer could a search engine, expert or experiment return?” If none exists, rename it from “research” to “uncertainty.”
rituals.twist: Notice which questions have no finite lookup answer.
rituals.mindBend: Not every question is a research task. Some are uncertainty wearing glasses.
rituals.mind_bend: Not every question is a research task. Some are uncertainty wearing glasses.
rituals.why: Some loops persist because the mind keeps searching for an answer that the question cannot structurally provide.
rituals.reveal: Some loops persist because the mind keeps searching for an answer that the question cannot structurally provide.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Finish this pass after the planned comparison. More rounds are not automatically more accurate and can become reassurance checking. Stop at the planned endpoint rather than repeating the ritual until it feels completely convincing.

rituals.name: SHOELACE START
rituals.goal: We are not “doing the task.”
rituals.mission: We are not “doing the task.”
rituals.rule: Guess whether the tiniest physical start changes motivation even one point.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether the tiniest physical start changes motivation even one point.
rituals.play: Choose a start smaller than the task: open the document, put shoes on, place the form on the desk, stand beside the sink. Do only that. Rate motivation before and after.
rituals.twist: Look for any change after motion begins rather than before.
rituals.mindBend: You may not need motivation to start; starting may be one way motivation gets made.
rituals.mind_bend: You may not need motivation to start; starting may be one way motivation gets made.
rituals.why: Motivation often follows contact with a task instead of politely arriving first.
rituals.reveal: Motivation often follows contact with a task instead of politely arriving first.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the chosen example within an ordinary safe task. A micro-step should reduce friction, not bypass limits, needed rest or a high-stakes decision process. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.

rituals.name: CROSS THE DOORWAY
rituals.goal: Move your body into the task zone before your brain holds another meeting.
rituals.mission: Move your body into the task zone before your brain holds another meeting.
rituals.rule: Guess whether crossing one physical boundary will make the task feel more real or more impossible.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether crossing one physical boundary will make the task feel more real or more impossible.
rituals.play: Choose the doorway, desk, kitchen, car, shower or room connected to the task. Cross into that space and stop. You are allowed to do nothing else.
rituals.twist: Notice how the decision changes once your body has already changed context.
rituals.mindBend: Sometimes the first decision is not “do it.” It is “stand where doing it happens.”
rituals.mind_bend: Sometimes the first decision is not “do it.” It is “stand where doing it happens.”
rituals.why: Physical context can cue action before motivation or certainty catches up.
rituals.reveal: Physical context can cue action before motivation or certainty catches up.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the chosen example small, reversible and safe. Do not use momentum as a reason to ignore pain, exhaustion, major consequences or information that needs more thought. If the same pattern returns later, re-check the new context rather than copying today's answer.

rituals.name: TWO-MINUTE DECOY
rituals.goal: Offer your brain a deal so small it suspects a scam.
rituals.mission: Offer your brain a deal so small it suspects a scam.
rituals.rule: Guess whether starting for only two minutes feels less threatening than “finish it.”
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether starting for only two minutes feels less threatening than “finish it.”

rituals.name: FEELING GETS ONE VOTE
rituals.goal: Your feeling gets a vote.
rituals.mission: Your feeling gets a vote.
rituals.rule: Guess how the decision changes when three voters speak: feeling, facts, values.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how the decision changes when three voters speak: feeling, facts, values.
rituals.play: For one choice, write three one-line votes: “Feeling wants…”, “Facts say…”, “Values point toward…”. Don’t average them yet.
rituals.twist: Check if the emotion becomes information rather than the whole decision.
rituals.mindBend: Feelings deserve a seat at the table, not automatic ownership of the building.
rituals.mind_bend: Feelings deserve a seat at the table, not automatic ownership of the building.
rituals.why: Emotions carry data and urgency, but decisions can integrate more than one information source.
rituals.reveal: Emotions carry data and urgency, but decisions can integrate more than one information source.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE

rituals.name: WHAT JOB IS ANGER DOING?
rituals.goal: Do not calm the anger yet.
rituals.mission: Do not calm the anger yet.
rituals.rule: Guess which job fits best: protect a boundary, restore fairness, create distance, or similar.
rituals.one_rule: Guess which job fits best: protect a boundary, restore fairness, create distance, or similar.
rituals.play: Finish: “If this irritation were useful, it would be trying to ____.” Then name one non-destructive way to perform that job.
rituals.twist: Check if the emotion becomes more specific once its function is named.
rituals.mindBend: You do not have to obey an emotion to learn what it is trying to protect.
rituals.mind_bend: You do not have to obey an emotion to learn what it is trying to protect.

rituals.name: URGE HAND / VALUE HAND
rituals.goal: Let the urge exist without making it the steering wheel.
rituals.mission: Let the urge exist without making it the steering wheel.
rituals.rule: Guess which hand moves first when you imagine the next thirty seconds.
rituals.one_rule: Guess which hand moves first when you imagine the next thirty seconds.
rituals.play: Put one hand forward for the immediate urge and one for the longer-term value. Move both hands slightly in the direction each wants.
rituals.twist: Notice that action can align with one system while the other system is still present.
rituals.mindBend: Alignment is choosing a direction while competing signals are still talking.
rituals.mind_bend: Alignment is choosing a direction while competing signals are still talking.
rituals.why: You do not need an urge to disappear before acting beside it.
rituals.reveal: You do not need an urge to disappear before acting beside it.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the hand movements small and comfortable. This is a choice check, not a command to obey an urge or push through pain. Stop if the movement feels physically uncomfortable or the urge points toward something unsafe.

rituals.name: FORECAST OR PREFERENCE?
rituals.goal: Your brain may be answering “Will it happen?”
rituals.mission: Your brain may be answering “Will it happen?”
rituals.rule: Guess which sentence is actually stronger in you: the forecast or the preference.
rituals.one_rule: Guess which sentence is actually stronger in you: the forecast or the preference.
rituals.play: Say both separately: “I predict ____ will happen.” Then: “I really don’t want ____ to happen.” Rate each sentence from 0–10 for certainty/intensity.
rituals.twist: Check if emotional intensity is being used as if it were probability evidence.
rituals.mindBend: Not wanting something is not evidence that it is coming.
rituals.mind_bend: Not wanting something is not evidence that it is coming.
rituals.why: Strong preference against an outcome can make the outcome feel more likely without adding predictive information.
rituals.reveal: Strong preference against an outcome can make the outcome feel more likely without adding predictive information.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use the sentence to separate feeling from interpretation, not to dismiss the feeling or any concrete need underneath it. Stop if the exercise makes you less steady. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.

rituals.name: BODY BEFORE BIOGRAPHY
rituals.goal: Give the body fifteen seconds before the autobiography begins.
rituals.mission: Give the body fifteen seconds before the autobiography begins.
rituals.rule: Guess which explanation your mind will try to add first.
rituals.one_rule: Guess which explanation your mind will try to add first.
rituals.play: For fifteen seconds, describe only location, size, temperature, movement, pressure and rhythm of the feeling. Every “because” gets deleted.
rituals.twist: Catch how urgently the brain tries to convert sensation into a story about your life.
rituals.mindBend: Your body can have a sensation without immediately publishing a biography about it.
rituals.mind_bend: Your body can have a sensation without immediately publishing a biography about it.
rituals.why: Observation and explanation are separate mental acts, even when they arrive almost together.
rituals.reveal: Observation and explanation are separate mental acts, even when they arrive almost together.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Do one short observation only; repeated symptom checking can feed the loop. Concerning or persistent physical symptoms are for medical assessment, not self-reassurance.

rituals.name: SIXTY-SECOND PERMISSION
rituals.goal: For one minute, the feeling is allowed to stay without being fixed.
rituals.mission: For one minute, the feeling is allowed to stay without being fixed.
rituals.rule: Guess what will happen if you stop trying to reduce it for sixty seconds.
rituals.one_rule: Guess what will happen if you stop trying to reduce it for sixty seconds.
rituals.play: Set 60 sec. Say: “You can be here until the timer ends.” Don’t feed the story, soothe, push away or measure every second.
rituals.twist: At the bell, notice what changed: intensity, location, texture, or only your struggle with it.
rituals.mindBend: You can dislike a feeling without turning its existence into an emergency.
rituals.mind_bend: You can dislike a feeling without turning its existence into an emergency.
rituals.why: Permission does not guarantee the feeling shrinks. It tests whether fighting it was adding a second layer.
rituals.reveal: Permission does not guarantee the feeling shrinks. It tests whether fighting it was adding a second layer.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the timed pass observational. The aim is not to prove the emotion wrong or force it away; practical needs and symptoms still deserve attention. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.

rituals.mindBend: A number can perform confidence. A choice has to use it.
rituals.mind_bend: A number can perform confidence. A choice has to use it.
rituals.why: When a belief has to guide a choice, confidence often becomes more honest.

rituals.name: SAME LIFE, NO TITLE
rituals.goal: Keep the daily reality.
rituals.mission: Keep the daily reality.
rituals.rule: Guess whether you would still choose the path if its title sounded ordinary.

rituals.twist: Separate attraction to the lived experience from attraction to the label.
rituals.mindBend: A title is packaging. Your life is what happens after you open the box.
rituals.mind_bend: A title is packaging. Your life is what happens after you open the box.
rituals.why: Status can make a path sparkle without changing what Tuesday afternoon feels like.

rituals.mission: Your character is not sitting a one-question final exam.

rituals.mind_bend: A mistake can require repair without becoming your permanent job title.

rituals.name: THE INVISIBLE MAINTENANCE DEPARTMENT
rituals.goal: Some of life’s meaning is hiding in jobs nobody applauds.
rituals.mission: Some of life’s meaning is hiding in jobs nobody applauds.
rituals.rule: Guess which tiny maintenance act would make tomorrow slightly kinder.
rituals.one_rule: Guess which tiny maintenance act would make tomorrow slightly kinder.
rituals.play: Choose one invisible act: refill something, send a check-in, put an item back, prep breakfast, charge a device, tidy one surface. Name who benefits—even if it is only future-you.
rituals.twist: Notice how meaning changes when you measure by service rather than drama.
rituals.mindBend: Quiet upkeep is still care, even when nobody claps.
rituals.mind_bend: Quiet upkeep is still care, even when nobody claps.
rituals.why: Maintenance rarely looks heroic because its success is often that nothing goes wrong.
rituals.reveal: Maintenance rarely looks heroic because its success is often that nothing goes wrong.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Send a check-in only where the relationship and timing make it appropriate. One message is enough; do not chase a response or use contact as proof that you are cared about.
rituals.precise_subpattern: Small maintenance dismissed as meaningless
rituals.preciseSubpattern: Small maintenance dismissed as meaningless
rituals.primary_trigger: Small maintenance dismissed as meaningless
rituals.challenge: Small maintenance dismissed as meaningless
rituals.recognition_cue: Small maintenance dismissed as meaningless
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Reframe mundane preventive action as service by explicitly identifying a beneficiary and prevented friction.

rituals.name: REGRET HAS TWO DIRECTIONS
rituals.goal: Regret keeps showing you one direction.
rituals.mission: Regret keeps showing you one direction.
rituals.rule: Guess which regret feels louder: doing the thing and disliking it, or never testing it at all.
rituals.one_rule: Guess which regret feels louder: doing the thing and disliking it, or never testing it at all.
rituals.play: Create two ten-second future scenes: “I tried and it was wrong for me,” then “I never tried and still wonder.” Don’t choose yet; just compare the emotional texture.
rituals.twist: Check if your mind had been simulating only one kind of regret.
rituals.mindBend: Not acting is also a decision with a future.
rituals.mind_bend: Not acting is also a decision with a future.
rituals.why: Avoidance often protects us from visible regret while hiding invisible regret.

PAUSE

rituals.twist: Use the reaction as information—not as a command.
rituals.mindBend: Sometimes you discover what you want when chance pretends to choose for you.
rituals.mind_bend: Sometimes you discover what you want when chance pretends to choose for you.

rituals.reveal: Randomness can reveal preference by removing the burden of choosing for one second.

rituals.name: MICRO-SWAY CAMERA
rituals.goal: Standing still is not actually still.
rituals.mission: Standing still is not actually still.
rituals.rule: If safe to stand, predict whether your body moves at all while you feel stationary.
rituals.one_rule: If safe to stand, predict whether your body moves at all while you feel stationary.
rituals.play: Stand comfortably near support if needed, or sit upright. Notice tiny forward-back or side-to-side sway for 10 sec. Don’t correct it.
rituals.twist: Catch movement that normally gets edited out of the idea of “still.”
rituals.mindBend: Stillness can be made of constant tiny corrections.
rituals.mind_bend: Stillness can be made of constant tiny corrections.
rituals.why: Balance is active adjustment, not frozen stability.
rituals.reveal: Balance is active adjustment, not frozen stability.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Do the movement once and keep the result provisional. If the exercise increases distress or confusion, stop rather than trying harder. If the same pattern returns later, re-check the new context rather than copying today's answer.

rituals.name: EYES CLOSED OBJECT CHECK
rituals.goal: Your eyes may be bossing the object around.
rituals.mission: Your eyes may be bossing the object around.
rituals.rule: Use a safe familiar object. Guess one detail your fingers will notice that your eyes ignored.
rituals.one_rule: Use a safe familiar object. Guess one detail your fingers will notice that your eyes ignored.
rituals.play: Close your eyes for five seconds while holding the object. Find one texture, edge or temperature detail. Open them again.
rituals.twist: Check if the object feels newly detailed.
rituals.mindBend: Reality gets richer when one sense stops monopolising the report.
rituals.mind_bend: Reality gets richer when one sense stops monopolising the report.
rituals.why: Different senses sample different information from the same thing.
rituals.reveal: Different senses sample different information from the same thing.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Close your eyes only while seated at a clear, stable surface. Keep the hand movement slow and use only a clean, blunt object if one is involved; reopen your eyes if you feel dizzy or disoriented.

rituals.challenge: Visual dominance overshadowing touch
rituals.recognition_cue: Visual dominance overshadowing touch
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Temporarily remove vision during safe object exploration to reveal tactile features suppressed by visual dominance.

rituals.name: INTERVAL CHECK
rituals.goal: We’re taking snapshots, not filming the whole feeling.
rituals.mission: We’re taking snapshots, not filming the whole feeling.
rituals.rule: Guess whether the sensation will be identical across three ten-second-spaced checks.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether the sensation will be identical across three ten-second-spaced checks.
rituals.play: Check one body sensation now. Look away mentally for 10 sec. Check again. Repeat once more. Use only same / stronger / weaker / shifted.
rituals.twist: Compare the three snapshots.
rituals.mindBend: You do not need to watch a sensation constantly to discover that it moves.
rituals.mind_bend: You do not need to watch a sensation constantly to discover that it moves.
rituals.why: Continuous-feeling states can vary between samples.
rituals.reveal: Continuous-feeling states can vary between samples.

PAUSE

rituals.name: TURN THE ROOM
rituals.goal: Move only your head and the sensory world reorganises.
rituals.mission: Move only your head and the sensory world reorganises.
rituals.rule: Guess which direction contains the most sound or visual activity.
rituals.one_rule: Guess which direction contains the most sound or visual activity.
rituals.play: Slowly turn your head left, centre, right once. At each point, notice one different sound or visual detail. Keep the body still if comfortable.
rituals.twist: Notice how changing orientation changes what becomes salient.
rituals.mindBend: Sometimes “the world feels intense” includes where your sensors are pointed.
rituals.mind_bend: Sometimes “the world feels intense” includes where your sensors are pointed.
rituals.why: The environment can feel different because the sampling angle changed.
rituals.reveal: The environment can feel different because the sampling angle changed.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Turn your head only a small, comfortable amount and keep the rest of your body stable. Stop immediately for neck pain, dizziness, nausea, visual disturbance or a change in balance.

rituals.preciseSubpattern: Head direction shaping sensory field
rituals.primary_trigger: Head direction shaping sensory field
rituals.challenge: Head direction shaping sensory field
rituals.recognition_cue: Head direction shaping sensory field
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Systematically change head orientation while sampling one new sensory feature per angle to expose viewpoint-dependent salience.

rituals.mission: The whole message may be boiling because of one word.
rituals.rule: Guess which single word is carrying the most heat.
rituals.one_rule: Guess which single word is carrying the most heat.
rituals.play: Take your draft or remembered sentence. Remove one loaded word—always, ridiculous, selfish, obviously, never, disrespectful—without changing the request.
rituals.twist: Notice how much temperature drops while the core point survives.
rituals.mindBend: You can keep the boundary and lower the flame.
rituals.mind_bend: You can keep the boundary and lower the flame.
rituals.why: Conflict can be amplified by one evaluative word rather than the whole message.
rituals.reveal: Conflict can be amplified by one evaluative word rather than the whole message.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Let the example you picked create possibilities, not excuses. Keep direct words, consent, patterns of behaviour and your own boundaries in the picture. Keep the result tied to this one example rather than generalising it to every situation.

rituals.name: SECRET CONTRACT
rituals.goal: They broke a script they may never have received.
rituals.mission: They broke a script they may never have received.
rituals.rule: Guess what exact behaviour you expected without explicitly asking for it.
rituals.one_rule: Guess what exact behaviour you expected without explicitly asking for it.

rituals.twist: Check if disappointment contains a hidden contract.
rituals.mindBend: An invisible agreement is still invisible to the other person.
rituals.mind_bend: An invisible agreement is still invisible to the other person.
rituals.why: Expectations can feel shared simply because they are obvious to us.
rituals.reveal: Expectations can feel shared simply because they are obvious to us.

PAUSE

rituals.name: CURIOSITY VERSION
rituals.goal: Let’s see whether the sentence is trying to learn or trying to convict.
rituals.mission: Let’s see whether the sentence is trying to learn or trying to convict.
rituals.rule: Guess how the other person would answer differently to an accusation versus a genuine question.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how the other person would answer differently to an accusation versus a genuine question.
rituals.play: Take “Why did you ignore me?” and convert only the unknown part into curiosity: “What happened after I messaged?” Keep the issue intact.
rituals.twist: Check if the new wording leaves room for information you do not already possess.
rituals.mindBend: Curiosity can protect your boundary while reopening access to facts.
rituals.mind_bend: Curiosity can protect your boundary while reopening access to facts.
rituals.why: Questions stop being questions when the verdict is baked into them.
rituals.reveal: Questions stop being questions when the verdict is baked into them.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use the example you picked to loosen assumptions about another person, not to overwrite what they actually said or did. Repeated harmful behaviour and stated boundaries still count. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.

rituals.name: GIFT OR INVOICE?

rituals.name: MAKE QUITTING TAKE TWO CLICKS

rituals.twist: Check if the extra step separates genuine change of mind from momentary avoidance.
rituals.mindBend: You can keep freedom while making quitting a conscious action.
rituals.mind_bend: You can keep freedom while making quitting a conscious action.
rituals.why: Small commitment devices create space between impulse and abandonment.
rituals.reveal: Small commitment devices create space between impulse and abandonment.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE

rituals.name: BORROW A WITNESS
rituals.goal: Some tasks start easier when another human exists nearby.
rituals.mission: Some tasks start easier when another human exists nearby.
rituals.rule: Guess whether you would begin faster if someone silently watched you start.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether you would begin faster if someone silently watched you start.
rituals.play: Imagine a trusted person sitting nearby for 60 sec, or use a real body-doubling setup if available. Your only job is to begin one visible action.
rituals.twist: Check if imagined or actual co-presence changes activation.
rituals.mindBend: Sometimes you do not need advice. You need a witness to the first move.
rituals.mind_bend: Sometimes you do not need advice. You need a witness to the first move.
rituals.why: Human presence can alter arousal and task engagement even without help.
rituals.reveal: Human presence can alter arousal and task engagement even without help.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use the mental image to reduce mind-reading, not to manufacture reassurance. Direct communication and boundaries carry more weight than guessed motives. If the same pattern returns later, re-check the new context rather than copying today's answer.

rituals.name: DON’T DELETE THE DONE
rituals.goal: Your task list keeps deleting evidence that you move.
rituals.mission: Your task list keeps deleting evidence that you move.
rituals.rule: Guess whether motivation changes when completed items stay visible for one session.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether motivation changes when completed items stay visible for one session.

rituals.twist: Check if the next action feels like continuation rather than starting from zero.
rituals.mindBend: A finished step can become momentum if you let it remain visible.
rituals.mind_bend: A finished step can become momentum if you let it remain visible.

rituals.name: TOMORROW’S FIRST MINUTE
rituals.goal: Do not picture the whole future benefit.
rituals.mission: Do not picture the whole future benefit.
rituals.rule: Guess the first tiny inconvenience future-you avoids if you act now.
rituals.one_rule: Guess the first tiny inconvenience future-you avoids if you act now.
rituals.play: Imagine tomorrow at the exact moment the benefit arrives: clean mug ready, email already sent, bag packed, document started. Describe only that first relieved minute.
rituals.twist: Check if the reward becomes more concrete.
rituals.mindBend: Future-you becomes easier to care about when they have a scene, not a slogan.
rituals.mind_bend: Future-you becomes easier to care about when they have a scene, not a slogan.
rituals.why: Near, specific consequences motivate differently from vague future benefits.
rituals.reveal: Near, specific consequences motivate differently from vague future benefits.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE

rituals.name: BETWEEN TWO THINGS
rituals.goal: Your new habit needs neighbours.
rituals.mission: Your new habit needs neighbours.
rituals.rule: Guess which two existing routines could sandwich it.
rituals.one_rule: Guess which two existing routines could sandwich it.
rituals.play: Choose an action that already happens before and one that happens after. Place the new behaviour between them: coffee → medication → shower, for example.
rituals.twist: Notice how the habit gains a fixed slot instead of floating in the day.
rituals.mindBend: A habit sticks better when it knows who comes before and after.
rituals.mind_bend: A habit sticks better when it knows who comes before and after.
rituals.why: Sequences are easier to retrieve when actions have stable neighbours.
rituals.reveal: Sequences are easier to retrieve when actions have stable neighbours.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use medication only as the middle cue if it is already prescribed or otherwise safely directed for that time. Do not change the dose, timing, route or storage instructions to make the sequence fit.

rituals.name: WHAT DOES IT WANT PROTECTED?

rituals.mission: Your emotion may be guarding something specific.

rituals.twist: Check if the feeling becomes information about a value or need.
rituals.mindBend: A feeling can be a guard dog without being the judge.
rituals.mind_bend: A feeling can be a guard dog without being the judge.
rituals.why: Emotions often organise attention around what seems threatened or important.
rituals.reveal: Emotions often organise attention around what seems threatened or important.

PAUSE

rituals.goal: Intensity and duration are different axes.
rituals.mission: Intensity and duration are different axes.

rituals.name: THE MISSING DENOMINATOR
rituals.goal: Three bad moments sounds enormous until we ask: three out of how many?
rituals.mission: Three bad moments sounds enormous until we ask: three out of how many?
rituals.rule: Guess the total number of comparable moments in the same period.
rituals.one_rule: Guess the total number of comparable moments in the same period.
rituals.play: Write the scary count on top: 3, 5, 10—whatever it is. Under it, estimate the total opportunities it came from. Turn it into “3 out of 40,” not just “3.”
rituals.twist: Check if the numerator shrinks emotionally when its denominator appears.
rituals.mindBend: A number without its denominator is wearing platform shoes.
rituals.mind_bend: A number without its denominator is wearing platform shoes.
rituals.why: Counts feel bigger when the background population is invisible.
rituals.reveal: Counts feel bigger when the background population is invisible.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the written version separate from genuine risk assessment: uncertainty can be reframed; clear danger should be acted on. Stop at the planned endpoint rather than repeating the ritual until it feels completely convincing.
rituals.precise_subpattern: A small count feeling huge because the total pool is ignored

rituals.challenge: A small count feeling huge because the total pool is ignored
rituals.recognition_cue: A small count feeling huge because the total pool is ignored
rituals.theory_backbone: Denominator neglect; risk perception; ratio reasoning
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Pair an emotionally salient event count with its previously omitted reference total to expose magnitude inflation from denominator blindness.

rituals.name: EYES CLOSED SIZE SHIFT
rituals.goal: Your body has a size map even when your eyes are off duty.
rituals.mission: Your body has a size map even when your eyes are off duty.
rituals.rule: Guess how large your hands feel with eyes open versus closed.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how large your hands feel with eyes open versus closed.
rituals.play: Look at one hand for three seconds. Close your eyes and feel only its boundaries for five seconds. Open and compare the sensed hand with the seen hand.
rituals.twist: Notice any shift in size, shape, weight, or vividness.
rituals.mindBend: What you feel as “my body” is an ongoing negotiation between signals.
rituals.mind_bend: What you feel as “my body” is an ongoing negotiation between signals.
rituals.why: The brain builds body experience from multiple senses that do not always agree perfectly.
rituals.reveal: The brain builds body experience from multiple senses that do not always agree perfectly.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the eyes-closed interval brief and stationary. Do not combine it with walking, driving, stairs or reaching around, and stop if you become dizzy or disoriented.

rituals.name: THREE TEXTURES, NO OPINIONS
rituals.goal: For thirty seconds, textures are facts, not reviews.
rituals.mission: For thirty seconds, textures are facts, not reviews.
rituals.rule: Guess which of three nearby surfaces will feel most different from the others.
rituals.one_rule: Guess which of three nearby surfaces will feel most different from the others.
rituals.play: Touch three safe surfaces. Describe each using only physical words: smooth, ridged, cool, soft, sticky, hard, grainy. Ban “nice,” “gross,” “annoying.”
rituals.twist: Check if sensory detail expands when evaluation is removed.
rituals.mindBend: A sensation can be specific before it becomes a verdict.
rituals.mind_bend: A sensation can be specific before it becomes a verdict.
rituals.why: Evaluation compresses experience into good/bad; description reopens detail.
rituals.reveal: Evaluation compresses experience into good/bad; description reopens detail.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use three ordinary clean surfaces that are safe to touch. Keep pressure light and skip anything sharp, sticky from an unknown substance, irritating, or unusually hot/cold.

rituals.name: TURN YOUR EARS
rituals.goal: Your ears have geometry.
rituals.mission: Your ears have geometry.
rituals.rule: Guess whether a steady sound changes when you turn your head slightly.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether a steady sound changes when you turn your head slightly.
rituals.play: Choose a constant safe sound. Slowly turn your head a little left, centre, right. Notice volume, direction, or clarity changes.
rituals.twist: Catch how the same sound is reconstructed from different angles.
rituals.mindBend: Sometimes the world did not change; your receiving angle did.
rituals.mind_bend: Sometimes the world did not change; your receiving angle did.
rituals.why: Perception changes with position even when the source does not.
rituals.reveal: Perception changes with position even when the source does not.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the head movement small, slow and comfortable, with stable support nearby if needed. Stop with neck pain, dizziness, nausea, visual disturbance or any balance change.

rituals.name: COUNT THE CUTS
rituals.goal: Your visual movie has more edits than you think.
rituals.mission: Your visual movie has more edits than you think.
rituals.rule: Guess how many times you blink in twenty seconds.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how many times you blink in twenty seconds.

rituals.twist: Catch how perception stitches over every cut.
rituals.mindBend: Your brain can hide interruptions so well that continuity feels absolute.
rituals.mind_bend: Your brain can hide interruptions so well that continuity feels absolute.
rituals.why: Conscious experience is smoother than the raw sensory stream.

PAUSE

rituals.rule: Guess whether one mild neutral sensation feels larger after ten seconds of focused attention.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether one mild neutral sensation feels larger after ten seconds of focused attention.

rituals.twist: Compare the sensation’s apparent size or importance across the two attention widths.
rituals.mindBend: Bigger in awareness is not automatically bigger in the body.
rituals.mind_bend: Bigger in awareness is not automatically bigger in the body.
rituals.why: Attention can magnify a sensation without changing its underlying cause.

rituals.goal: That judgment may have your handwriting on it.
rituals.mission: That judgment may have your handwriting on it.

rituals.name: HOW MANY ORIGINAL OPINIONS?

rituals.mission: Ten people agreeing may contain fewer than ten independent judgments.
rituals.rule: Guess how many of the opinions could have been influenced by earlier opinions.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how many of the opinions could have been influenced by earlier opinions.
rituals.play: Take the crowd signal bothering you. Imagine person 2 saw person 1, person 3 saw the first two, and so on. Ask how many truly independent data points might remain.
rituals.twist: Notice how consensus strength changes when influence between people is allowed.
rituals.mindBend: A crowd can echo one signal many times.
rituals.mind_bend: A crowd can echo one signal many times.
rituals.why: Agreement is weaker evidence when opinions are socially linked.
rituals.reveal: Agreement is weaker evidence when opinions are socially linked.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the example you picked on the interpretation, not the other person's rights or limits. A kinder explanation does not cancel a clear no, repeated harm or needed distance. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.

rituals.name: ANSWER ONLY THIS WEEK
rituals.goal: Your mind wants a forever answer to a seven-day problem.
rituals.mission: Your mind wants a forever answer to a seven-day problem.
rituals.rule: Guess whether the question changes if it only needs to be good for one week.

rituals.mindBend: Not every uncertainty needs a lifetime contract.
rituals.mind_bend: Not every uncertainty needs a lifetime contract.

PAUSE

rituals.name: REHEARSAL OR FAN FICTION?
rituals.goal: You may be rehearsing a person who does not exist yet.
rituals.mission: You may be rehearsing a person who does not exist yet.
rituals.rule: Guess how many lines in your imagined conversation belong to the other person rather than you.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how many lines in your imagined conversation belong to the other person rather than you.
rituals.play: Replay the scene. Put brackets around every sentence you invented for them. Keep only your own possible opening line.
rituals.twist: Notice how much of the rehearsal depended on controlling both characters.
rituals.mindBend: Preparation ends where the other person’s unscripted mind begins.
rituals.mind_bend: Preparation ends where the other person’s unscripted mind begins.
rituals.why: Imagined conversations feel useful because you get to write every response.
rituals.reveal: Imagined conversations feel useful because you get to write every response.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use only a memory you can revisit without becoming overwhelmed. Do not force missing details or repeatedly replay the scene; stop if you feel flooded, detached, unreal, disoriented or pulled into a flashback.

rituals.name: WHAT WOULD COUNT AS ENOUGH?
rituals.goal: Your search has no finish line because “enough” was never defined.
rituals.mission: Your search has no finish line because “enough” was never defined.
rituals.rule: Guess what specific piece of information would genuinely change your decision.
rituals.one_rule: Guess what specific piece of information would genuinely change your decision.
rituals.play: Before searching again, write one stopping rule: “I stop when I know ___,” or “after two reliable sources,” or “after 20 minutes.”
rituals.twist: Check if the urge to keep searching survives even after the rule is met.
rituals.mindBend: You can finish a search before you feel finished.
rituals.mind_bend: You can finish a search before you feel finished.
rituals.why: Information seeking becomes a loop when the stopping condition is emotional certainty.
rituals.reveal: Information seeking becomes a loop when the stopping condition is emotional certainty.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep this pass to one planned pass. Do not keep adding evidence until you feel perfectly certain; uncertainty is allowed to remain. Leave room for new evidence after the exercise instead of treating the result as final.

rituals.name: THOUGHT QUALITY CURFEW
rituals.goal: Your brain may be open after the thinking department has closed.
rituals.mission: Your brain may be open after the thinking department has closed.
rituals.rule: Guess when your reasoning usually gets repetitive: late, hungry, exhausted, after conflict, after long work.
rituals.one_rule: Guess when your reasoning usually gets repetitive: late, hungry, exhausted, after conflict, after long work.
rituals.play: Choose one recurring low-quality window. Make a rule: “No life verdicts in this state; only notes for tomorrow.”
rituals.twist: Notice how different the loop feels when it loses decision authority.
rituals.mindBend: More thinking at the wrong time is not automatically better thinking.
rituals.mind_bend: More thinking at the wrong time is not automatically better thinking.
rituals.why: Cognitive fatigue can increase repetition while reducing flexibility.
rituals.reveal: Cognitive fatigue can increase repetition while reducing flexibility.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the chosen example small, reversible and safe. Do not use momentum as a reason to ignore pain, exhaustion, major consequences or information that needs more thought. Keep the result tied to this one example rather than generalising it to every situation.

75 sec

GAME
SOURCE CHECK THE FEELING

This feeling may have arrived from somewhere else and attached itself to the nearest story.

Feelings need a source check before they become explanations.

rituals.mission: A painful feeling can accompany a direction you still respect.
rituals.rule: Guess whether the action would matter to you even if it stayed uncomfortable.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether the action would matter to you even if it stayed uncomfortable.
rituals.play: Name the action and the feeling separately. Finish: “This feels ___, and it moves me toward ___.” Don’t force the feeling to agree.
rituals.twist: Check if discomfort and direction can coexist.
rituals.mindBend: Feeling bad does not automatically mean moving wrong.
rituals.mind_bend: Feeling bad does not automatically mean moving wrong.
rituals.why: Values and emotions answer different questions.
rituals.reveal: Values and emotions answer different questions.
rituals.safety:

rituals.mission: This mood is trying to edit yesterday and predict tomorrow.

rituals.twist: Check if the current state still feels like the only emotional climate available.
rituals.mindBend: Now is real. It is not the owner of the whole timeline.
rituals.mind_bend: Now is real. It is not the owner of the whole timeline.

PAUSE

rituals.name: RANDOMNESS HAS STREAKS
rituals.goal: Your brain sees three similar events and immediately hires a conspiracy board.
rituals.mission: Your brain sees three similar events and immediately hires a conspiracy board.
rituals.rule: Guess which looks more random: H-T-H-T-H-T or H-H-H-T-T-H.
rituals.one_rule: Guess which looks more random: H-T-H-T-H-T or H-H-H-T-T-H.
rituals.play: Imagine six coin tosses. Notice which sequence feels more random. Now remember that real randomness naturally produces runs, clumps and ugly streaks.
rituals.twist: Catch the discomfort when random does not look evenly mixed.
rituals.mindBend: A streak can be real without being a signal.
rituals.mind_bend: A streak can be real without being a signal.
rituals.why: We expect randomness to look more balanced than randomness actually looks.
rituals.reveal: We expect randomness to look more balanced than randomness actually looks.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the mental image light and reversible. The exercise should widen perspective, not pressure you to deny facts or push through rising distress. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.

rituals.primary_trigger: Crossed fingers confusing touch location
rituals.challenge: Crossed fingers confusing touch location
rituals.recognition_cue: Crossed fingers confusing touch location
rituals.theory_backbone: Aristotle illusion; tactile localisation; body schema
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Create an unusual crossed-finger geometry so one tactile object stimulates skin locations normally associated with two separate objects.
rituals.ritualText:
PLAY TIME
60 sec

GAME
TWO TOUCHES FROM ONE

GOAL
Your fingers can convince your brain that one object became two.

ONE RULE
Guess how one small round object will feel when touched between crossed fingertips.

PLAY
Cross your index and middle finger. Gently touch a small round object like a pen cap or marble between the crossed fingertips. Uncross and try again.

TWIST
Check if the crossed version creates an odd double-touch impression.

MIND BEND
Perception can be confidently wrong when the body is arranged unusually.

SAFETY
PAUSE
Use a clean, blunt, lightweight round object and only gentle fingertip pressure. Keep sharp, hot, breakable or very small objects away from the face, and stop if the fingers hurt, tingle or go numb.

rituals.mission: The object may feel lighter without losing a gram.

rituals.twist: Notice the contrast effect in your muscles and perception.
rituals.mindBend: Feeling lighter does not mean becoming lighter.
rituals.mind_bend: Feeling lighter does not mean becoming lighter.

rituals.reveal: Sensation is judged relative to what came immediately before.

rituals.name: FLOATING FINGER SAUSAGE
rituals.goal: Your eyes can build an object that is not there.
rituals.mission: Your eyes can build an object that is not there.
rituals.rule: Guess what appears between two fingertips when you focus past them.
rituals.one_rule: Guess what appears between two fingertips when you focus past them.
rituals.play: Hold both index fingertips facing each other a few centimetres apart in front of your face. Focus on something far beyond them.

rituals.mindBend: Seeing is construction, not just reception.
rituals.mind_bend: Seeing is construction, not just reception.
rituals.why: Each eye supplies a different view and the brain fuses them into one experience.
rituals.reveal: Each eye supplies a different view and the brain fuses them into one experience.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use the hold as a test, not a verdict. Stop if you begin forcing the result or using it to ignore information that clearly needs action. If the same pattern returns later, re-check the new context rather than copying today's answer.

rituals.name: COLOUR LEAVES BEFORE SHAPE
rituals.goal: Your peripheral vision is less colourful than it feels.
rituals.mission: Your peripheral vision is less colourful than it feels.
rituals.rule: Guess whether you lose colour or object shape first as something moves toward the edge of vision.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether you lose colour or object shape first as something moves toward the edge of vision.
rituals.play: Fix your gaze straight ahead. Move a colourful safe object slowly from beside your head toward the front without following it with your eyes. Notice when colour becomes clear.
rituals.twist: Catch that you can detect 'something' before you can identify its colour well.
rituals.mindBend: Your visual field feels uniformly detailed because the brain stitches unequal zones together.
rituals.mind_bend: Your visual field feels uniformly detailed because the brain stitches unequal zones together.
rituals.why: Peripheral vision prioritises different information than central vision.
rituals.reveal: Peripheral vision prioritises different information than central vision.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use a soft, lightweight object with no sharp edge and move it slowly without bringing it close to the eye. Keep your gaze comfortable and stop for eye strain, headache, dizziness or visual discomfort.

rituals.reveal: Attention selects some information at the cost of other available information.

rituals.mission: Your verbal loop needs a mouth-shaped workspace, even when silent.

rituals.theory_backbone: Denomination effect; mental accounting; spending psychology
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Hold monetary value constant while varying denomination structure to reveal representation-driven differences in spending friction.
rituals.ritualText:
PLAY TIME
65 sec

GAME
ONE FIFTY OR FIVE TENS?

GOAL
Same money, different psychological armour.

ONE RULE
Guess which feels harder to spend: one $50 note or five $10 notes.

PLAY
Imagine the exact same amount in one large unit versus several small units. Which version feels more 'breakable'?

TWIST
Catch how denomination changes spending friction without changing value.

MIND BEND
The number stayed the same; the spending threshold moved.

SAFETY
PAUSE
Keep the mental image observational. The aim is not to prove the emotion wrong or force it away; practical needs and symptoms still deserve attention. Keep the result tied to this one example rather than generalising it to every situation.

rituals.name: PRIVATE WEIRDNESS CLUB
rituals.goal: Your embarrassing reaction may be far less exclusive than your brain claims.
rituals.mission: Your embarrassing reaction may be far less exclusive than your brain claims.
rituals.rule: Guess what percentage of ordinary people would have some version of the same reaction.
rituals.one_rule: Guess what percentage of ordinary people would have some version of the same reaction.
rituals.play: Imagine ten people in the same situation. Give at least three of them plausible internal reactions similar to yours, even if they hide them differently.
rituals.twist: Check if the feeling becomes less like evidence of personal defect.
rituals.mindBend: Private weirdness is often public humanity with better camouflage.
rituals.mind_bend: Private weirdness is often public humanity with better camouflage.
rituals.why: We often underestimate how common our uncomfortable traits and reactions are.
rituals.reveal: We often underestimate how common our uncomfortable traits and reactions are.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Let the mental image create possibilities, not excuses. Keep direct words, consent, patterns of behaviour and your own boundaries in the picture. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.

70 sec

GAME
MORE THAN ONE TEAM JERSEY

GOAL
You belong to more than one room.

ONE RULE
Guess which identity group feels so loud that the others disappear.

PLAY
List five groups or communities you belong to in any sense: family, profession, culture, hobby, neighbourhood, generation, friendship circle, interest.

TWIST
Notice how no single jersey fully explains you.

You can belong strongly without belonging only.

SAFETY
PAUSE

rituals.name: RIGHT CAN STILL FEEL UNCERTAIN
rituals.goal: You may be waiting for certainty to certify a choice that certainty never certifies.
rituals.mission: You may be waiting for certainty to certify a choice that certainty never certifies.
rituals.rule: Guess how certain a genuinely good decision should realistically feel before its outcome exists.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how certain a genuinely good decision should realistically feel before its outcome exists.
rituals.play: Think of one past decision that worked out well. Remember how much uncertainty you had before making it.
rituals.twist: Check if good outcomes in your own history required perfect confidence.
rituals.mindBend: A good choice can arrive wearing doubt.
rituals.mind_bend: A good choice can arrive wearing doubt.
rituals.why: Decision quality and subjective certainty are only loosely linked.
rituals.reveal: Decision quality and subjective certainty are only loosely linked.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the memory/imagery pass to one planned pass. Do not keep adding evidence until you feel perfectly certain; uncertainty is allowed to remain. Keep the result tied to this one example rather than generalising it to every situation.

rituals.name: COMPLEMENTARY COLOUR ECHO
rituals.goal: Your eyes can keep a colour after the object is gone.
rituals.mission: Your eyes can keep a colour after the object is gone.
rituals.rule: Guess what colour ghost appears after staring at one safe coloured object.
rituals.one_rule: Guess what colour ghost appears after staring at one safe coloured object.
rituals.play: Look at a non-bright coloured object for about fifteen seconds, then shift to a plain white or light wall. Don’t use lights or the sun.
rituals.twist: Catch the faint complementary colour that may appear.
rituals.mindBend: Seeing something after it is gone can be a property of the visual system, not of the world.
rituals.mind_bend: Seeing something after it is gone can be a property of the visual system, not of the world.
rituals.why: Visual receptors adapt, and the contrast system keeps processing after the stimulus leaves.
rituals.reveal: Visual receptors adapt, and the contrast system keeps processing after the stimulus leaves.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use an ordinary non-glare object and a comfortable gaze; never use the sun, bright lamps, lasers or anything painful to look at. Stop for eye pain, headache, dizziness or a visual effect that lingers unexpectedly.
rituals.precise_subpattern: Recently viewed colour producing an opposite-colour percept after removal
rituals.preciseSubpattern: Recently viewed colour producing an opposite-colour percept after removal
rituals.primary_trigger: Recently viewed colour producing an opposite-colour percept after removal
rituals.challenge: Recently viewed colour producing an opposite-colour percept after removal
rituals.recognition_cue: Recently viewed colour producing an opposite-colour percept after removal
rituals.theory_backbone: Visual adaptation; opponent-process colour vision; afterimage
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Briefly adapt to a safe coloured surface, then view a neutral field to reveal a complementary afterimage caused by receptor/opponent adaptation.

65 sec

GAME
POP-OUT VS HUNT

GOAL
Some targets shout; others make attention search seat by seat.

ONE RULE
Guess what is easier to find: one red X among black Xs, or one red X among red Os and black Xs.

PLAY
Draw or imagine both displays. Notice how a single unique colour pops, while a target defined by colour plus shape needs more scanning.

TWIST
Catch the difference between automatic pop-out and deliberate search.

MIND BEND
Difficulty finding something can belong to the search design, not your effort.

SAFETY
PAUSE
Keep the sketch light and reversible. The exercise should widen perspective, not pressure you to deny facts or push through rising distress. Leave room for new evidence after the exercise instead of treating the result as final.

rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Translate a private prosocial intention into one externally observable behaviour that could communicate it to another person.
rituals.ritualText:
PLAY TIME
70 sec

GAME
YOUR INTENT NEEDS A DELIVERY VEHICLE

GOAL
You meant well.

ONE RULE
Guess which action or sentence would make the intention observable.

PLAY
Name the intention—care, respect, support, apology, appreciation. Name 1 behaviour that would let an outsider detect it.

TWIST
Notice the gap between privately having an intention and publicly transmitting it.

MIND BEND
Good intent matters, but it still needs a delivery vehicle.

SAFETY
PAUSE
Let the naming step create possibilities, not excuses. Keep direct words, consent, patterns of behaviour and your own boundaries in the picture. If the same pattern returns later, re-check the new context rather than copying today's answer.

rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Deliberately generate a harmless absurd action thought and observe that thought occurrence does not compel behaviour or imply endorsement.
rituals.ritualText:
PLAY TIME
70 sec

GAME
THOUGHT IS NOT A CONTRACT

GOAL
A sentence appeared in your mind.

ONE RULE
Guess whether thinking 'I could quit / shout / fail / embarrass myself' makes the action more physically inevitable.

PLAY
Say one harmless absurd thought on purpose: 'I could wear a saucepan as a hat.' Wait 10 sec and notice that no behaviour automatically follows.

TWIST
Catch the gap between mental content and action.

MIND BEND
Imagining an action is not signing the action.

SAFETY
PAUSE
Use the sentence for a low-stakes next step, not an irreversible decision. If the action has meaningful financial, medical, legal or safety consequences, slow down. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.

rituals.name: LET THE WORD FIND YOU

rituals.mission: The harder you chase the missing word, the more it hides behind the furniture.
rituals.rule: Guess whether the word is more likely to appear after thirty seconds of not searching.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether the word is more likely to appear after thirty seconds of not searching.
rituals.play: When a harmless name or word is stuck, note its first letter or category if known. Switch attention completely for 30 sec.
rituals.twist: Return once and see whether retrieval changed.
rituals.mindBend: Sometimes memory needs less chasing, not more effort.
rituals.mind_bend: Sometimes memory needs less chasing, not more effort.
rituals.why: Fixated retrieval attempts can keep activating the wrong competitors.
rituals.reveal: Fixated retrieval attempts can keep activating the wrong competitors.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE

rituals.goal: Once you chose, memory may have started campaigning for your side.
rituals.mission: Once you chose, memory may have started campaigning for your side.
rituals.rule: Guess which drawbacks of your chosen option became fuzzier after commitment.

rituals.twist: Check if memory had been tidying the choice after the fact.
rituals.mindBend: Peace after a decision can partly come from selective remembering.
rituals.mind_bend: Peace after a decision can partly come from selective remembering.
rituals.why: Memory often becomes more supportive of choices we already made.
rituals.reveal: Memory often becomes more supportive of choices we already made.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the memory/imagery pass tentative: memory can shift with attention and framing. Do not turn a recalled detail into certainty without independent evidence. If the same pattern returns later, re-check the new context rather than copying today's answer.

rituals.name: ONE ANSWER, NEXT DOUBT
rituals.goal: Let's test whether certainty actually has a finish line.
rituals.mission: Let's test whether certainty actually has a finish line.
rituals.rule: Guess the next doubt that would appear if your current question were answered perfectly.
rituals.one_rule: Guess the next doubt that would appear if your current question were answered perfectly.
rituals.play: Imagine receiving the exact answer you want. Immediately finish: 'Okay, but what if ___?'
rituals.twist: Catch how fast the goalpost can move.
rituals.mindBend: A moving finish line cannot be reached by running faster.
rituals.mind_bend: A moving finish line cannot be reached by running faster.
rituals.why: When the problem is intolerance of uncertainty, answers can generate new questions.
rituals.reveal: When the problem is intolerance of uncertainty, answers can generate new questions.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Do the mental image once, then stop. If it turns into repeated checking, recalculating or reassurance-seeking for certainty, the exercise has become the loop. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.
