rituals.name: CHANGE IT OR CARRY IT?
rituals.goal: Before regulating the feeling, check whether the situation itself is movable.
rituals.mission: Before regulating the feeling, check whether the situation itself is movable.
rituals.rule: Guess: is the main problem controllable now, partly controllable, or not controllable today?
rituals.one_rule: Guess: is the main problem controllable now, partly controllable, or not controllable today?
rituals.play: Put the issue in one box. CONTROLLABLE: choose 1 action. PARTLY: choose your piece. NOT NOW: choose one way to carry the feeling safely.
rituals.twist: Notice how the regulation strategy changes with controllability.
rituals.mindBend: Do not use acceptance on a fixable leak—or a wrench on the weather.
rituals.mind_bend: Do not use acceptance on a fixable leak—or a wrench on the weather.
rituals.why: Coping works better when strategy matches what can actually be changed.
rituals.reveal: Coping works better when strategy matches what can actually be changed.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE

rituals.name: NEW ROOM, OLD FEELING
rituals.goal: The context changed.
rituals.mission: The context changed.
rituals.rule: Guess how much of this feeling was already present before you entered the current situation.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how much of this feeling was already present before you entered the current situation.
rituals.play: Rate the emotion just before the context change and now. Ask what new evidence arrived in between.
rituals.twist: Check if the state persisted more than the facts changed.
rituals.mindBend: A feeling arriving in a new room is not proof the new room caused it.
rituals.mind_bend: A feeling arriving in a new room is not proof the new room caused it.
rituals.why: Emotions can have momentum across situations.
rituals.reveal: Emotions can have momentum across situations.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Let the rating change the story around the feeling without invalidating the feeling itself. If distress rises sharply, stop rather than push through. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.

rituals.name: ONE STORY BEAT THE DATA
rituals.goal: One fresh story can feel larger than a thousand boring numbers.

rituals.play: Write the frequency estimate you had before the story, then the estimate after. Compare that shift with whether any actual population data changed.
rituals.twist: Notice the story's emotional weight versus its statistical weight.
rituals.mindBend: A story can be memorable without being representative.
rituals.mind_bend: A story can be memorable without being representative.
rituals.why: Vivid examples can overpower base-rate information.
rituals.reveal: Vivid examples can overpower base-rate information.

rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Translate a holistic visual memory into detailed verbal features and compare the resulting representation with original visual familiarity.
rituals.ritualText:
PLAY TIME
65 sec

GAME
STOP DESCRIBING THE FACE

GOAL
Sometimes explaining what you saw makes recognition worse.

ONE RULE
Guess whether describing a face in detail helps you recognise it later.

PLAY
Think of a familiar face. Describe it in words for 20 sec, then imagine the face again. Notice whether the verbal description feels poorer than the visual whole.

TWIST
Catch the mismatch between verbal features and holistic recognition.

MIND BEND
Not every memory gets clearer when translated into words.

SAFETY
PAUSE
Keep the memory/imagery pass separate from fact-finding. A vivid or faint memory is not, by itself, proof of what happened. If the same pattern returns later, re-check the new context rather than copying today's answer.

rituals.ritual_name: THE HINTS CAN BLOCK THE REST
rituals.goal: Helpful hints can accidentally crowd the doorway.
rituals.mission: Helpful hints can accidentally crowd the doorway.
rituals.rule: Guess whether seeing half a list always helps you remember the other half.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether seeing half a list always helps you remember the other half.
rituals.play: Think of a category with many items—people at an event, errands, examples. First recall freely. Look at a partial list and try to recall what is missing.
rituals.twist: Check if the shown items dominate search.
rituals.mindBend: A hint can organise memory so strongly that alternatives become harder to reach.
rituals.mind_bend: A hint can organise memory so strongly that alternatives become harder to reach.
rituals.why: Partial cues can interfere with retrieval of related uncued information.
rituals.reveal: Partial cues can interfere with retrieval of related uncued information.
rituals.moveOn: ↻ THE HINTS CAN BLOCK THE REST
rituals.move_on: ↻ THE HINTS CAN BLOCK THE REST
rituals.safety:
PAUSE

rituals.name: FIRST MEMORIES TAKE THE OXYGEN
rituals.goal: The first answers out can make the later ones harder to find.
rituals.mission: The first answers out can make the later ones harder to find.
rituals.rule: Guess whether recall gets slower after several related items have already been produced.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether recall gets slower after several related items have already been produced.
rituals.play: Recall examples from one category for 30 sec. Notice the gap between early easy items and later struggling search.
rituals.twist: Catch how retrieval itself changes the field.
rituals.mindBend: The archive gets harder to search while you are emptying it.
rituals.mind_bend: The archive gets harder to search while you are emptying it.
rituals.why: Producing some memories can interfere with access to others.
rituals.reveal: Producing some memories can interfere with access to others.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Treat the memory/imagery pass as a memory exercise, not a reconstruction of objective proof. Do not fill missing detail just to make the story coherent. Keep the result tied to this one example rather than generalising it to every situation.

rituals.displayName: DID YOU INVENT IT OR REMEMBER IT?
rituals.name: DID YOU INVENT IT OR REMEMBER IT?
rituals.ritual_name: DID YOU INVENT IT OR REMEMBER IT?
rituals.goal: A familiar idea can return without its source tag and feel brand new.
rituals.mission: A familiar idea can return without its source tag and feel brand new.
rituals.rule: Guess whether you've encountered this idea before in a conversation, article, video, or old note.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether you've encountered this idea before in a conversation, article, video, or old note.
rituals.play: Take a sudden 'original' idea. Search your own recent memory for possible source exposures before claiming novelty.
rituals.twist: Notice how idea familiarity can survive after source memory fades.
rituals.mindBend: Original-feeling is not proof of original origin.
rituals.mind_bend: Original-feeling is not proof of original origin.
rituals.why: Content memory can outlast memory of where content came from.
rituals.reveal: Content memory can outlast memory of where content came from.
rituals.moveOn: ↻ DID YOU INVENT IT OR REMEMBER IT?
rituals.move_on: ↻ DID YOU INVENT IT OR REMEMBER IT?
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the example you picked tentative: memory can shift with attention and framing. Do not turn a recalled detail into certainty without independent evidence. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.

rituals.name: FAMILIARITY WITHOUT A FILE
rituals.goal: Sometimes the feeling of familiarity arrives without a matching memory file.
rituals.mission: Sometimes the feeling of familiarity arrives without a matching memory file.
rituals.rule: Guess whether 'this feels familiar' always means you can retrieve a specific earlier event.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether 'this feels familiar' always means you can retrieve a specific earlier event.
rituals.play: When a harmless déjà-vu-like familiarity occurs, separate FAMILIAR FEELING from RETRIEVABLE MEMORY. Ask what exact prior event you can name.
rituals.twist: Check if the signal exists without a source.
rituals.mindBend: A familiarity signal can be real even when the story attached to it is uncertain.
rituals.mind_bend: A familiarity signal can be real even when the story attached to it is uncertain.
rituals.why: Familiarity and recollection are separable memory processes.
rituals.reveal: Familiarity and recollection are separable memory processes.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Treat this pass as a memory exercise, not a reconstruction of objective proof. Do not fill missing detail just to make the story coherent. Keep the result tied to this one example rather than generalising it to every situation.

rituals.name: RECALL BEFORE REVIEW
rituals.goal: Rereading feels smooth.
rituals.mission: Rereading feels smooth.
rituals.rule: Guess what you can remember before looking again.
rituals.one_rule: Guess what you can remember before looking again.
rituals.play: Close the note and write three things you remember. Reopen and correct.
rituals.twist: Notice how the missing pieces become more memorable after effortful retrieval.
rituals.mindBend: Struggle can be the part that teaches.
rituals.mind_bend: Struggle can be the part that teaches.
rituals.why: Retrieval practice strengthens later access more than passive restudy alone.
rituals.reveal: Retrieval practice strengthens later access more than passive restudy alone.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use this pass to examine recall, not to force a definitive version of the past. Missing or changing details are allowed to stay uncertain. Leave room for new evidence after the exercise instead of treating the result as final.
rituals.precise_subpattern: Trying to retrieve information strengthening memory more than rereading
rituals.preciseSubpattern: Trying to retrieve information strengthening memory more than rereading
rituals.primary_trigger: Trying to retrieve information strengthening memory more than rereading
rituals.challenge: Trying to retrieve information strengthening memory more than rereading
rituals.recognition_cue: Trying to retrieve information strengthening memory more than rereading
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Attempt unaided recall before restudy, then compare and correct against the source.

rituals.name: MAKE PRACTICE A LITTLE UGLY
rituals.goal: If practice feels perfect, your brain may be doing too little.
rituals.mission: If practice feels perfect, your brain may be doing too little.
rituals.rule: Guess which change makes retrieval harder but still possible.
rituals.one_rule: Guess which change makes retrieval harder but still possible.
rituals.play: Add one gentle difficulty: remove hints, increase spacing, mix examples, explain from memory, use a blank page.
rituals.twist: Check if performance feels worse while thinking becomes deeper.
rituals.mindBend: Easy today and remembered tomorrow are not the same target.
rituals.mind_bend: Easy today and remembered tomorrow are not the same target.
rituals.why: Some difficulties improve long-term learning despite reducing short-term fluency.
rituals.reveal: Some difficulties improve long-term learning despite reducing short-term fluency.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use this pass as a test, not a verdict. Stop if you begin forcing the result or using it to ignore information that clearly needs action. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.

rituals.preciseSubpattern: Easy fluency mistaken for better learning

rituals.challenge: Easy fluency mistaken for better learning
rituals.recognition_cue: Easy fluency mistaken for better learning
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Introduce one manageable challenge to practice that reduces immediate fluency while increasing active retrieval or discrimination.

rituals.name: WRONG WITH CONFIDENCE CAN TEACH
rituals.goal: A confident mistake can become excellent glue for the correction.
rituals.mission: A confident mistake can become excellent glue for the correction.
rituals.rule: Guess which wrong answer you were most certain about.
rituals.one_rule: Guess which wrong answer you were most certain about.
rituals.play: Write the confident wrong answer and the correct answer side by side. Add 1 line explaining exactly why the first one fails.
rituals.twist: Notice how surprise makes the correction sticky.
rituals.mindBend: Being confidently wrong can create a memorable update—if you actually update.
rituals.mind_bend: Being confidently wrong can create a memorable update—if you actually update.
rituals.why: High-confidence errors can produce strong correction learning.
rituals.reveal: High-confidence errors can produce strong correction learning.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use the written version as a test, not a verdict. Stop if you begin forcing the result or using it to ignore information that clearly needs action. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.

rituals.name: DON'T PLAY MEMORY WHACK-A-MOLE
rituals.goal: Fighting a memory can turn the session into nothing but memory-monitoring.
rituals.mission: Fighting a memory can turn the session into nothing but memory-monitoring.
rituals.rule: Guess how often you must check for the memory to know you're successfully 'not thinking' it.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how often you must check for the memory to know you're successfully 'not thinking' it.
rituals.play: For one harmless intrusive memory, replace 'Don’t remember' with 'I notice the memory is available; I'm returning to X.' No checking whether it left.
rituals.twist: Notice the drop in monitoring work.
rituals.mindBend: You cannot verify a memory is absent without searching for it.
rituals.mind_bend: You cannot verify a memory is absent without searching for it.
rituals.why: Intentional suppression requires monitoring for the target and can become effortful or paradoxical.
rituals.reveal: Intentional suppression requires monitoring for the target and can become effortful or paradoxical.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use this pass to calibrate confidence, not to reach 100% certainty. Stop if you notice yourself repeating it just to feel sure. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.

rituals.primary_trigger: Trying not to retrieve a memory altering later accessibility
rituals.challenge: Trying not to retrieve a memory altering later accessibility
rituals.recognition_cue: Trying not to retrieve a memory altering later accessibility
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Replace active target-memory suppression and absence-checking with acknowledgment followed by attention return, removing the monitoring loop.

rituals.theory_backbone: Undoing effect; positive emotion; physiological recovery
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Introduce a mild safe positive emotional cue after ordinary negative arousal and observe recovery in bodily activation without reframing the stressor.
rituals.ritualText:
PLAY TIME
70 sec

GAME
HELP THE BODY LAND

GOAL
You do not need to become happy; sometimes a small positive cue helps the body come down.

ONE RULE
Guess if a small pleasant cue helps your body settle after mild stress.

PLAY
After an ordinary stressful moment, spend one minute with something mildly positive and safe—warm interaction, humour, nature, music—without denying the stress.

TWIST
Check if breathing, posture, or pace settles.

MIND BEND
A small good feeling can help the body finish a stress cycle without erasing what happened.

SAFETY
PAUSE
Keep this pass observational. The aim is not to prove the emotion wrong or force it away; practical needs and symptoms still deserve attention. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.

rituals.ritualText:

75 sec

GAME
BAD OUTCOME, FAKE MORAL CAUSE?

GOAL
After unfairness, the brain may restore order by blaming the person.

Take a harmless unlucky outcome. List one behavioural cause, one situational cause, and one chance cause before judging deservingness.

Check if moral explanation was appearing faster than causal evidence.

A fair world is comforting; inventing guilt does not make it fair.

PAUSE

rituals.ritual_name: CROSS YOUR FINGERS, DOUBLE THE OBJECT
rituals.goal: Crossed fingers can scramble the brain’s touch map.
rituals.mission: Crossed fingers can scramble the brain’s touch map.
rituals.rule: Guess whether you can identify which crossed fingertip was tapped without looking.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether you can identify which crossed fingertip was tapped without looking.
rituals.play: Cross your index and middle finger. Close your eyes while seated.
rituals.twist: Check if touch location is easier once your fingers return to normal.
rituals.mindBend: Touch is not just where the signal lands; it is where your body map expects it to land.
rituals.mind_bend: Touch is not just where the signal lands; it is where your body map expects it to land.
rituals.why: The brain combines skin input with its usual map of finger position, so unusual geometry can distort localization.
rituals.reveal: The brain combines skin input with its usual map of finger position, so unusual geometry can distort localization.
rituals.moveOn: ↻ CROSS YOUR FINGERS, DOUBLE THE OBJECT
rituals.move_on: ↻ CROSS YOUR FINGERS, DOUBLE THE OBJECT
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Do this seated with clean hands and very light taps only. Keep your hands away from the face and eyes, stop if any finger hurts, tingles or goes numb, and keep eyes open if closing them makes you dizzy.

rituals.name: THE RING RESIZES THE CENTRE
rituals.goal: Same centre circle. New frame. New apparent size.
rituals.mission: Same centre circle. New frame. New apparent size.
rituals.rule: Guess whether a tight ring or a wide ring makes the same centre look larger.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether a tight ring or a wide ring makes the same centre look larger.
rituals.play: Draw one centre circle. Add a tight outer ring and look. Cover the ring, then redraw a much wider ring around the same centre. Compare before measuring.
rituals.twist: Notice whether the centre seems to resize when only the ring gap changes.
rituals.mindBend: Your eyes can edit size without moving a single edge of the thing you are judging.
rituals.mind_bend: Your eyes can edit size without moving a single edge of the thing you are judging.
rituals.why: Changing the surrounding contour can shift apparent size while the target stays physically identical.
rituals.reveal: Changing the surrounding contour can shift apparent size while the target stays physically identical.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use the sketch as a test, not a verdict. Stop if you begin forcing the result or using it to ignore information that clearly needs action. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.

rituals.name: BORDER BRIGHTNESS HACK
rituals.goal: A tiny boundary can make entire regions look lighter or darker.
rituals.mission: A tiny boundary can make entire regions look lighter or darker.
rituals.rule: Guess whether two broad grey areas with equal centres can look different if their shared edge has a light-dark gradient.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether two broad grey areas with equal centres can look different if their shared edge has a light-dark gradient.
rituals.play: Imagine two equal grey panels touching, with a narrow bright strip on one side of the border and dark strip on the other. Cover the edge mentally or physically.
rituals.twist: Catch the large-area brightness difference collapse when the edge disappears.
rituals.mindBend: A narrow edge can colour your experience of a huge area.
rituals.mind_bend: A narrow edge can colour your experience of a huge area.
rituals.why: The visual system infers surface brightness strongly from local edge structure.
rituals.reveal: The visual system infers surface brightness strongly from local edge structure.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Keep the mental image light and reversible. The exercise should widen perspective, not pressure you to deny facts or push through rising distress. Leave room for new evidence after the exercise instead of treating the result as final.

rituals.name: THE WHEEL CAN TURN BACKWARD
rituals.goal: Continuous forward motion can look backward when your visual samples land at the wrong rhythm.
rituals.mission: Continuous forward motion can look backward when your visual samples land at the wrong rhythm.
rituals.rule: Guess how a wheel looks under flicker or video when each frame resembles an earlier spoke position.
rituals.one_rule: Guess how a wheel looks under flicker or video when each frame resembles an earlier spoke position.
rituals.play: Imagine a wheel rotating slightly less than one spoke spacing between snapshots. Track which spoke your brain matches across frames.
rituals.twist: Catch apparent reversal emerge from matching.
rituals.mindBend: Motion direction can be an inference from samples, not a direct copy of movement.
rituals.mind_bend: Motion direction can be an inference from samples, not a direct copy of movement.
rituals.why: Discrete temporal sampling can create aliasing in motion perception.
rituals.reveal: Discrete temporal sampling can create aliasing in motion perception.
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use the mental image to expose a bias, not to generate a decision-grade statistic. Important choices still need reliable numbers and context. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.

rituals.preciseSubpattern: Repeated visual sampling making continuous rotation appear slower, still, or reversed

rituals.recognition_cue: Repeated visual sampling making continuous rotation appear slower, still, or reversed
rituals.theory_backbone: Wagon-wheel effect; temporal aliasing; motion perception
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Sample repetitive rotational positions at intervals that cause successive spokes to be matched with earlier positions, producing apparent reversal.

rituals.mindBend: More attention can masquerade as more time.
rituals.mind_bend: More attention can masquerade as more time.

PAUSE

Even meaningless words arrive with perceptual baggage.

rituals.ritualText:
PLAY TIME
70 sec

GAME
WHAT IF THIS IS ONE OF THE LAST TEN?

GOAL
Ordinary things become visible when an ending appears.

ONE RULE
Guess how differently you would notice this routine if you knew you had only ten more of them.

PLAY
Choose something benign and recurring—a school pickup, route, lunch place, team ritual, child's bedtime story. Imagine only ten remain.

TWIST
Notice which details suddenly matter.

MIND BEND
Scarcity of future repetitions can make the present repetition visible.

SAFETY
PAUSE
Use the chosen example as a test, not a verdict. Stop if you begin forcing the result or using it to ignore information that clearly needs action. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.

rituals.mindBend: Good intentions are not enough if the support type is wrong.
rituals.mind_bend: Good intentions are not enough if the support type is wrong.

rituals.goal: People often remember whether they felt understood before they remember your brilliant advice.

rituals.mind_bend: Connection often begins with 'you make sense to me,' not 'here is the fix.'

rituals.safety:

rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Construct a response that separately communicates understanding, validation and care before offering problem-solving.
rituals.ritualText:
PLAY TIME
70 sec

GAME
THREE SIGNALS OF 'I GET YOU'

GOAL
People often remember whether they felt understood before they remember your brilliant advice.

ONE RULE
Guess which signal is missing: understood, validated, cared for.

PLAY
In one supportive reply, include one line for each needed signal: 'I hear X,' 'that makes sense because Y,' 'I'm with you / what would help?'

TWIST
Notice how the response feels different from jumping to solutions.

MIND BEND
Connection often begins with 'you make sense to me,' not 'here is the fix.'

SAFETY
PAUSE
Offer only support you genuinely mean and can sustain. Do not promise availability, agreement or responsibility you cannot give, and respect the other person's privacy and boundaries.

70 sec

GAME

Current-you likes to recruit past-you into today's opinion.

rituals.why: Sadness carries loss appraisals that can influence unrelated valuation.

rituals.displayName: PAUSE THE GOOD THING ON PURPOSE
rituals.name: PAUSE THE GOOD THING ON PURPOSE
rituals.ritual_name: PAUSE THE GOOD THING ON PURPOSE
rituals.goal: Continuous pleasure can fade into background.
rituals.mission: Continuous pleasure can fade into background.
rituals.rule: Guess whether your favourite song, snack, view, or show is more noticeable after a short interruption.
rituals.one_rule: Guess whether your favourite song, snack, view, or show is more noticeable after a short interruption.
rituals.play: During one ordinary pleasant activity, pause for 30 sec and return. Compare enjoyment before and after the break.
rituals.twist: Catch attention renew on re-entry.
rituals.mindBend: A small break can increase contact with something good instead of reducing it.
rituals.mind_bend: A small break can increase contact with something good instead of reducing it.
rituals.why: Interruptions can disrupt hedonic adaptation and renew attention to positive experiences.
rituals.reveal: Interruptions can disrupt hedonic adaptation and renew attention to positive experiences.
rituals.moveOn: ↻ PAUSE THE GOOD THING ON PURPOSE
rituals.move_on: ↻ PAUSE THE GOOD THING ON PURPOSE
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Do this pass once and keep the result provisional. If the exercise increases distress or confusion, stop rather than trying harder. The result is a working perspective, not proof that the opposite story is true.

rituals.preciseSubpattern: Continuous pleasant exposure fading into the background through adaptation

rituals.recognition_cue: Continuous pleasant exposure fading into the background through adaptation
rituals.unique_game_move: PAUSE THE GOOD THING ON PURPOSE
rituals.theory_backbone: Hedonic adaptation disruption; positive experience; attention
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Insert a brief neutral interruption into a continuing mild positive experience and compare enjoyment immediately before versus after resumption.

rituals.name: HAVE YOU TESTED A LEVER?
rituals.goal: The sentence 'nothing helps' can shut down experiments before they start.
rituals.mission: The sentence 'nothing helps' can shut down experiments before they start.
rituals.rule: Guess one part of the state you might influence without controlling the whole emotion.
rituals.one_rule: Guess one part of the state you might influence without controlling the whole emotion.
rituals.play: Choose one lever only: body body activation, attention, interpretation, environment, action urge, social contact. Test it for two minutes.
rituals.twist: Check if any component moves even if the emotion stays.
rituals.mindBend: You do not need total emotional control for one lever to work.
rituals.mind_bend: You do not need total emotional control for one lever to work.
rituals.why: Beliefs about regulation capacity influence strategy use and persistence.
rituals.reveal: Beliefs about regulation capacity influence strategy use and persistence.
rituals.moveOn: ↻ CAN'T CHANGE IT OR HAVEN'T TESTED A LEVER?
rituals.move_on: ↻ CAN'T CHANGE IT OR HAVEN'T TESTED A LEVER?
rituals.safety:
PAUSE
Use the chosen example to separate feeling from interpretation, not to dismiss the feeling or any concrete need underneath it. Stop if the exercise makes you less steady. A single pass can test the pattern; it does not need to settle it permanently.

rituals.theory_backbone: Emotion regulation self-efficacy; control beliefs; regulation
rituals.mechanism_fingerprint: Replace a global uncontrollability judgment with a brief test of one specific modifiable component of the emotional episode.

rituals.name: STATE OR PROCESS?
rituals.goal: If you think feelings are fixed objects, you wait.
rituals.mission: If you think feelings are fixed objects, you wait.

rituals.name: PUT ORDINARY TUESDAY BACK IN THE FUTURE
rituals.ritual_name: PUT ORDINARY TUESDAY BACK IN THE FUTURE
rituals.goal: Your forecast contains the event in HD and everyday life in invisible ink.
rituals.mission: Your forecast contains the event in HD and everyday life in invisible ink.
rituals.rule: Guess what you will actually be doing three days after the outcome: breakfast, messages, work, errands, people, sleep.
rituals.one_rule: Guess what you will actually be doing three days after the outcome: breakfast, messages, work, errands, people, sleep.
